source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: March 31, 1849, in The Flag of Our Union (Boston)

source.excerpt:
Take this kiss upon the brow!
And, in parting from you now,
Thus much let me avow—
You are not wrong, who deem
That my days have been a dream;
Yet if hope has flown away
In a night, or in a day,
In a vision, or in none,
Is it therefore the less gone?
All that we see or seem
Is but a dream within a dream.
trail: The poem evolved through two earlier drafts — “Imitation” (1827) and “To——” (1829) — before Poe rewrote it almost entirely into the 1849 version, as detailed in the Poe Society’s Mabbott edition notes ↗.
It first reached print in the Boston Flag of Our Union on March 31, 1849, per the Wikipedia publication history ↗.
The exact text, matching the newspaper printing, is preserved in the 1859 collected Works of the Late Edgar Allan Poe on Wikisource ↗.
source.excerptNote: The line is repeated, in altered interrogative form, at the end of the poem’s second stanza as well.

source.rightsNote: First published in 1849, well before the U.S. public-domain cutoff of 1931, so the poem — and this line from it — carries no copyright restriction.

author.bio: Poe was a central figure of American Romanticism and Gothic fiction, celebrated for poems and stories steeped in mystery and melancholy. “A Dream Within a Dream” is among his most quoted shorter poems, meditating on the fleeting, illusory nature of time and hope.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: “A Dream Within a Dream” reached its final, familiar form late in Poe’s life — a manuscript from 1849 — after two earlier drafts under different titles stretching back to 1827. Poe died just months after its publication.

The poem’s closing image, of grains of sand slipping through a clenched fist on a “surf-tormented shore,” became one of the most anthologized meditations on loss and the unreality of experience in American poetry, and the couplet “All that we see or seem / Is but a dream within a dream” is now widely circulated on its own, detached from the poem.
